analysis.one_liner: Strips money damages and lawyer fees from lawsuits over government religious displays.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee after its Republican sponsor and 30 cosponsors never moved it past a House Judiciary subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal civil rights law so that a person who sues over a government religious display — a Ten Commandments monument, a religious seal, a prayer at a government meeting — could only get a court order, not money damages, and could not recover attorney fees if they won. It applies to state and local governments, and separately to the federal government. Courts award attorney fees to winning civil rights plaintiffs precisely because many people cannot afford to sue a government on their own; removing that fee recovery would make most of these cases too expensive to bring.
analysis.who_benefits: Governments and officials who want to keep religious monuments, seals, prayers, and references on public buildings and currency. Under current law a government that loses an Establishment Clause lawsuit can be ordered to pay the winning plaintiff's attorney fees; this bill removes that exposure and removes the deterrent of money judgments, letting challenged displays stay up through years of litigation. Taxpayers would avoid paying damages and fee awards in these specific suits.

how_it_helps.text: Limits remedies in Establishment Clause lawsuits against state and local officials to court orders (injunctive and declaratory relief), including for monuments, buildings, official seals, and prayers in legislative bodies [S2][S3].
Bars attorney fee awards to prevailing plaintiffs in those state and local government cases [S2][S3].
Applies the same limits to suits against the United States and federal officials, covering federal buildings, currency, the Pledge, and official seals [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who object to government religious endorsements — often religious minorities or nonbelievers — would lose their practical ability to enforce the Establishment Clause. Without money damages or fee recovery, most individuals cannot afford lawyers for a case that yields only an injunction, so unconstitutional displays would effectively face no legal check.

drawbacks.text: Removing attorney fee awards would price most individual plaintiffs out of these cases entirely, since a lawyer cannot be paid for a case that yields only an order against the government [S2].
The bill applies retroactively to any case already pending when it took effect, wiping out claims and fee requests mid-litigation [S3].

Limiting remedies for constitutional violations to injunctions weakens deterrence generally: a government with no money at stake has little incentive to remove a display a court has already found unconstitutional.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would save governments money in these specific lawsuits, and its supporters view taxpayer-funded damages for religious-display suits as an abuse of the courts. But the savings come entirely from making constitutional rights harder to enforce: the people who pay are those whose only tool against an unconstitutional government religious display is a lawsuit they could no longer afford. There is no compensating benefit to ordinary people in the bill's text.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee in February 2019, moved to a subcommittee in March, and stayed there until Congress ended in January 2021 without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Johnson (R-LA) introduced the bill on February 14, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
On March 25, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where no further action was recorded [S5].
Thirty House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat cosponsored it [S4].
The House never voted on the bill and the 116th Congress ended without it advancing [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's failure preserved the existing right to sue governments over religious endorsements and to recover attorney fees when winning, so citizens and civil rights plaintiffs are better off than they would have been if it passed. The governments it would have shielded gained nothing, but lost nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Citizens who keep their right to sue

for.name: Rep. Mike Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 30 Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee in March 2019 and never reported it back for a House vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-controlled House.

industries.note: Governments would no longer owe money damages or attorney fees when they lose Establishment Clause suits over monuments, seals, or prayers, removing the main financial incentive to comply with the Constitution. That gain comes directly out of the enforceability of citizens' rights.
The federal government and its officials would face the same remedy limits and fee bar, saving money in Establishment Clause litigation. The saving again comes from shrinking citizens' remedies.

industries.industry: Civil rights attorneys and plaintiffs' bar
industries.note: Attorney fee awards are what make these cases financially viable to bring; ending them would dry up most representation for citizens challenging government religious endorsements.
